analogy.p: A forecast says there is a 30% chance of rain each day. Over 100 days the forecaster would expect about 30 rainy days, but you would not be shocked by 27 or 34. Expected frequency works the same way: probability gives the prediction for a large number of tries, and chance causes real counts to wobble around it. The analogy breaks down because in a real forecast the weather on one day can affect the next, whereas expected outcomes in maths questions assume trials are independent.

bullets: **Expected frequency** is the predicted number of times an event will occur in a number of trials.
A **trial** is one go at the experiment (one roll, one spin, one day of weather data).
The expected frequency is a **long-run average**, so it does not have to be a whole number.
It links the idea of probability (a number between 0 and 1) to real counts of things.
It is used for fairness checks, planning (how many people will turn up) and predicting from surveys and samples.
The word "expect" in a question is a signal to use the formula P x n.
core.p: An **expected outcome** (also called an **expected frequency**) is the number of times you would predict an event to happen if an experiment were repeated a given number of times, using its probability. It is a prediction based on probability, not a promise of what will actually happen. If you roll a fair die 60 times, you would expect about 10 sixes because the probability of a six is 1/6, but in a real set of 60 rolls you might get 7 or 13. Edexcel Higher tier expects you to calculate expected outcomes, to compare them with actual results, and to explain what the comparison tells you.

bullets: Expected frequency = P(event) x n, where n is the number of trials.
Rearranged: n = expected frequency / P(event).
Rearranged: P(event) = expected frequency / n.
Check units and context: the answer is a **count** of things, not a probability.
Example: P(late) = 0.08 over 250 days gives 0.08 x 250 = 20 late days.
Example: to expect 12 sixes with a fair die you need n = 12 / (1/6) = 12 x 6 = 72 rolls.
Always write the calculation, because a correct method scores marks even if the arithmetic slips.
core.h: The formula: expected frequency = probability x number of trials
core.p: The core rule is that **expected frequency = probability of the event x number of trials**. This works because probability is the fraction of trials in which the event is predicted to occur, so multiplying that fraction by the total number of trials gives the predicted count. For example if P(green) = 0.3 and a spinner is spun 250 times, the expected number of greens is 0.3 x 250 = 75. You can use the probability as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage as long as you convert correctly (a percentage is divided by 100 first). The formula can be rearranged to find the number of trials or the probability when the other two are known.

bullets: Count the total outcomes first, then the favourable outcomes.
Use **P(not A) = 1 - P(A)** when it is quicker.
The probabilities of all the possible outcomes of an experiment add up to **1** (they are **exhaustive**).
Replacement means the probability is the same for each trial, so P x n works directly.
Simplify fractions only at the end, or use a calculator with the fraction left as it is, to avoid rounding errors.
If a question gives odds or ratios, convert to a probability first (a ratio 2 : 3 gives 2/5).
core.p: Often the probability is not given and you must work it out. If outcomes are equally likely, **probability = number of successful outcomes / total number of outcomes**. In a bag with 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters there are 10 counters, so P(blue) = 3/10. If a counter is picked and replaced 80 times, the expected number of blues is 3/10 x 80 = 24. You must be careful that the probability is for the **event asked about**, for example "not green" is 1 - 2/10 = 8/10, and that the trials are independent (the probability stays the same on each trial).

bullets: **Relative frequency = frequency of event / total frequency.**
It is also called **experimental probability**.
Use it when you cannot work out the theoretical probability.
Example: 110 sixes in 500 rolls gives relative frequency 110/500 = 0.22.
A larger sample reduces the effect of chance and gives a better estimate.
Relative frequencies for all outcomes in one experiment add up to 1 (check this).
Do not round the relative frequency too early; keep it as a fraction or decimal until the final step.
core.h: Using relative frequency to estimate probability
core.p: When outcomes are not equally likely, or the situation is too complicated to count (a biased die, a weighted coin, whether a drawing pin lands point up), you **estimate probability from an experiment** using **relative frequency**. Relative frequency = number of times the event happened / total number of trials. Then you use that estimate in the formula. If a biased die is rolled 500 times and a six occurs 110 times, the estimated P(six) = 110/500 = 0.22, so in 300 rolls you would expect 0.22 x 300 = 66 sixes. The estimate is only as good as the experiment, so more trials give a more reliable estimate.

bullets: A graph of relative frequency against number of trials **wobbles at first then settles**.
Early values can be far from the true probability.
It does **not** mean the results "even out" or that a coin is "due" a head after tails (each toss is independent).
To improve reliability: **increase the number of trials** (and make sure the experiment is fair).
The true probability is the value the relative frequency approaches.
Two experiments with the same number of trials can still give different results, which is normal.
core.h: Why more trials give better estimates
core.p: The **law of large numbers** says that as the number of trials increases, the relative frequency tends to get closer to the true (theoretical) probability. With few trials, chance has a big effect, so the relative frequency can be far from the true value. For example after 10 throws of a fair coin you could easily see 8 heads (relative frequency 0.8), but after 500 throws it will usually be very close to 0.5. This is why exam questions say that a bigger sample or more repeats makes the estimate more reliable, and it is the reason a graph of relative frequency against number of trials settles down.

bullets: **Actual frequency** = what was observed in the experiment.
Expected and actual rarely match exactly because of chance.
Small differences = consistent with a fair situation.
Large differences = evidence of **bias** (for example a die loaded towards six).
Compare using numbers: "6 occurred 110 times but about 83 were expected for a fair die".
Never say you have proved a die is biased from a single experiment.
Check that the actual frequencies add to the total number of trials.
core.p: The expected frequency tells you what to predict; the **actual frequency** is what really happened. They are rarely identical because of **random variation**. In 60 rolls of a fair die each face is expected 10 times, but actual results such as 8, 12, 9, 11, 13 and 7 (which add to 60) are perfectly normal. Differences that are small compared with the expected value are normal. Differences that are very large, or that appear again and again over many trials, suggest the die might be **biased**. In exam answers you should compare the actual with the expected number and make a conclusion that uses words such as "suggests" or "evidence", not "proves".

bullets: A **fair** die has P(each face) = 1/6.
**Biased** means the outcomes are not equally likely.
Expected for a fair die in n rolls: n/6 per face (state decimals to 1 d.p. if not whole).
Compare each result with the expected, and look for any much bigger or smaller.
Suggest improving the test by **repeating with more trials**.
Say "this suggests the die is biased" rather than "it is definitely biased".
A single experiment with few rolls is not strong evidence.
core.p: A question may ask whether a die, coin or spinner is **fair** (all outcomes **equally likely**). Work out the expected frequency for a fair object, compare it with the actual results, and decide. For a fair die rolled 500 times each face is expected 500/6 = 83.3 times. If a six comes up 110 times, that is 26.7 more than expected, a large difference, which suggests the die may be biased towards six. A better test would repeat the experiment with many more throws and see whether six still appears more often than expected.

bullets: **P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)** for independent events.
Two fair coins: HH, HT, TH, TT each have probability 1/4.
Expected number of HH in 200 throws = 1/4 x 200 = 50.
From a tree diagram, multiply along the branches then by n.
For "either/or" outcomes add the probabilities of the separate paths first (the **OR rule** for mutually exclusive outcomes).
Check the total: the expected frequencies of all outcomes add to n.
core.h: Two or more events and tree diagrams
core.p: Expected frequencies work with combined events too. First find the probability of the combined outcome (using the **AND rule** for independent events, multiply the probabilities, or by listing outcomes), then multiply by the number of trials. With two fair coins, P(two heads) = 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4, so in 200 throws of the pair you would expect 1/4 x 200 = 50 double heads. The same works for dependent events from a tree diagram: multiply along the branches to get the probability of the path, then multiply by n.

bullets: Estimate probability from the **sample proportion**.
Scale up: expected = sample proportion x population size.
A sample must be **random** and **representative** to be reliable.
A bigger sample gives a better estimate.
From a two-way table use the correct total (row, column or overall) for the probability asked.
State the answer as an **estimate**, for example "about 360 students".
core.h: Expected outcomes from tables, surveys and samples
core.p: You can also use expected frequency to **scale up** from a sample to a bigger population. If 18 of a sample of 60 students walk to school, the estimated probability that a student walks is 18/60 = 0.3, so out of 1200 students you would expect 0.3 x 1200 = 360 to walk. The estimate is more reliable when the sample is large and **representative** (random, not just one year group). Two-way tables give relative frequencies in the same way: choose the correct row or column total as the denominator.

bullets: Give the answer as a **number of things**, with context (for example "about 75 greens").
Do not round until the end.
Probabilities as decimals, fractions or percentages are all fine; **convert percentages** (35% = 0.35).
A probability is always between 0 and 1; an expected frequency can be larger than 1.
If asked for a whole number, round sensibly (people cannot be 31.5).
Write the calculation line so that a method mark can be awarded.
core.h: Rounding, units and the language of answers
core.p: Expected frequencies are **predictions**, so write "about" or "approximately" and give the answer in context. If the calculation gives 31.5 days of rain from 0.35 x 90 you may write 31.5, or round to about 32 days if the question asks for a whole number of days. A count of people or objects is usually rounded to a whole number; do not round in the middle of a calculation. Mark schemes often award the method mark for the correct multiplication P x n and the accuracy mark for the correct final value with a sensible rounding.

bullets: **Type 1:** P x n directly.
**Type 2:** rearrange to n = expected / P.
**Type 3:** relative frequency first, then P x n.
**Type 4:** compare expected with actual and write a conclusion.
**Type 5:** use words such as chance, random variation and sample size.
Show every step because several marks are for method.
Always check that your final answer is sensible (not greater than n).
core.h: Common question types and how to approach them
core.p: Edexcel questions on expected outcomes fall into a few types: (1) given probability and n, find the expected number; (2) find n from an expected number; (3) estimate probability from an experiment then predict a new expected number; (4) judge fairness by comparing expected and actual; (5) explain why the actual result differs from the expected. Reading the question for the word "expect", the number of trials, and whether outcomes are equally likely will point you to the method quickly.

bullets: Fractions, decimals and percentages: converting probabilities.
Sample spaces and Venn diagrams give the probabilities to multiply.
Tree diagrams give the probability of combined events.
Frequency tables and two-way tables give relative frequencies.
Sampling: larger random samples give more reliable estimates.
Biology link: a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio predicts about 75 dominant offspring from 100.
Higher tier extension: expected frequencies from conditional probabilities and dependent events.
core.p: Expected outcomes pull together several areas of the Edexcel specification. They use **fractions, decimals and percentages** to represent probability, the **sample space and listing outcomes**, the **AND and OR rules** and **tree diagrams**, and they connect to **statistics** through sampling and frequency tables. In science courses the same idea appears when predicting results of genetic crosses (a 3 : 1 ratio becomes an expected number of offspring) and when explaining that real results vary from predictions.

bullets: Without replacement the probabilities change, so be careful using P x n over many trials.
Combined outcomes: multiply along branches, then multiply by n.
If probabilities involve algebra, set up and solve an equation.
Probabilities of mutually exclusive, exhaustive outcomes sum to 1; use this to find a missing probability, then multiply by n.
Expected frequency can be given in terms of n (for example n/4).
A reasoning question may ask you to compare two sets of results with different numbers of trials, so use **relative frequencies** not raw counts.
core.h: Higher tier extension and tricky cases
core.p: At Higher tier, expected outcomes may be combined with **dependent events** (without replacement) and with **algebra**. If the probability depends on an unknown x, for example P(red) = x/(x + 7), you form an equation using the expected number and solve it. Remember that without replacement the probability changes after each pick, so P x n does not apply across repeated picks from the same bag; instead you use the tree diagram probability for the combined outcome. Questions may also give the probabilities as an algebraic expression and ask for the expected frequency in terms of n.

exam: **Command words:** "Work out an estimate" and "Work out the expected number" both need P x n with the working shown.
**1-2 marks:** one method mark for P x n (for example 0.3 x 250) and one accuracy mark for the answer 75.
**3 marks:** estimate P from relative frequency (1 mark), multiply by n (1 mark), correct answer (1 mark).
**Fairness (2-3 marks):** state the expected value, compare it with the actual value, and give a conclusion using "suggests".
**Explaining differences:** use the phrase "the results vary due to chance / random variation".
**Improving reliability:** "do more trials" or "use a larger sample".
**Rearranging:** n = expected / P. Write the line of working.
**Check:** relative frequencies must add to 1 and expected frequencies must add to n.
**Rounding:** give a whole number for people or objects; use "about" in the sentence.
**Show all working:** wrong answers can still earn method marks.

mistakes.r: It is a prediction; actual results vary because of chance.
mistakes.w: Expected frequency is the number that will definitely happen.

mistakes.r: Multiply: expected frequency = probability x number of trials.
mistakes.w: Adding the probability to the number of trials.

mistakes.r: Give a number of things in context, such as 75 greens.
mistakes.w: Writing the answer as a probability (for example 0.3) instead of a count.

mistakes.r: Each trial is independent; relative frequency approaches the probability only over many trials.
mistakes.w: After tails a head is due, so results even out.

mistakes.r: Convert the percentage to a decimal or fraction first.
mistakes.w: Using a percentage as 35 instead of 0.35.

mistakes.r: Say the results suggest bias and recommend more trials.
mistakes.w: Saying the die is definitely biased from one experiment.

mistakes.r: Divide by the number of trials to get relative frequency, then compare.
mistakes.w: Using the count instead of relative frequency when comparing samples of different sizes.

mistakes.r: Keep fractions or full calculator values until the final step.
mistakes.w: Rounding the probability early, such as 0.33 for 1/3.

summary: You need to calculate the expected number of times an event will happen, using probability x number of trials, estimate probabilities from relative frequency, and compare expected with actual results to judge fairness. It matters because it appears in most Edexcel probability papers and tests reasoning as well as calculation.

terms.d: The number of times an event is predicted to occur in a given number of trials, found using probability x number of trials.
One repeat of an experiment, such as one roll of a die.
A number from 0 to 1 that measures how likely an event is.
The number of times an event happens divided by the total number of trials; used to estimate probability.
A probability estimated from the results of an experiment (relative frequency).
A probability worked out from equally likely outcomes: favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
A set of events that includes all possible outcomes, so their probabilities add to 1.
Events that cannot happen at the same time.
Events where the outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other.
Differences in results caused by chance.
A selection taken from a population, used to estimate something about the whole.
A sample that reflects the make-up of the whole population.

worked.q: A spinner has P(green) = 0.3. It is spun 250 times. Work out the expected number of greens. [2 marks]
steps: Expected frequency = probability x number of trials.

worked.ans: (a) 0.22 (b) 66 sixes (c) Yes, the results suggest bias because 110 is far more than the 83.3 expected; more rolls would give more reliable evidence.
worked.q: A biased die is rolled 500 times and a six occurs 110 times. (a) Estimate P(six). (b) Predict the number of sixes in 300 rolls. (c) Does the result suggest the die is biased? [5 marks]
steps: (c) A fair die has P(six) = 1/6, so in 500 rolls expect 500/6 = 83.3 sixes.
The actual 110 is much larger than 83.3, so the die may be biased towards six.

worked.q: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters. A counter is picked, its colour noted and it is replaced. This is done 80 times. How many blue counters would you expect? [2 marks]
